statement: In children aged 6 to 14 with ADHD who were taking stimulant medicine and took more than an hour to fall asleep (27 or 28 children in the run-in phase of a trial in a Vancouver hospital ADHD programme; Weiss et al., 2006), a sleep-routine programme (a regular bedtime and waking time, no caffeine and no naps, worked out with parents from sleep diaries), compared with the same children's sleep before it, is associated with falling asleep sooner: from 91.7 to 69.3 minutes on parents' diaries and from 98.1 to 73.0 minutes on wrist activity monitors (effect size 0.67), with less variation from night to night on the diaries. Only 5 children then fell asleep within an hour, clinicians rated 21% much or very much improved and 54% unchanged, and ADHD ratings did not change. There was no comparison group, so part of the change may have happened anyway, for example because children were chosen when their sleep was at its worst. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: Families of children on ADHD medicine who took over an hour to fall asleep kept a set bedtime and waking time and cut out caffeine and naps. Afterwards the children fell asleep a little over 20 minutes sooner than before, but only 5 of them fell asleep within an hour. There was no comparison group, so some of this change might have happened anyway.
population: Children aged 6 to 14 with ADHD on stable stimulant medicine taking more than 60 minutes to fall asleep, in a hospital ADHD programme
exposure: A sleep-hygiene programme: a consistent bedtime and waking time, no caffeine and no naps, reviewed with parents from sleep diaries (study conditions in the study card)
comparator: The same children's sleep in the nights before the programme (no control group)
outcome: Time to fall asleep (parent diaries and actigraphy), night-to-night variability, clinician-rated improvement, ADHD symptoms
magnitude: Sleep-onset latency 91.7 to 69.3 minutes on diaries (t(28) = 2.77, p = .01) and 98.1 to 73.0 on actigraphy (t(21) = 2.92, p < .01); effect size 0.67; diary variability 47.7 to 29.1 minutes; 5 children below 60 minutes; clinicians: 21% much or very much improved, 54% unchanged.

evidence.locator: Method › Sample, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Procedures › Sleep Hygiene
evidence.extracted: Inclusion required stimulant medicine at an unchanged dose and a mean sleep-onset latency over 60 minutes on 10 nights of parent diaries; sleep hygiene meant reviewing the diaries with parent and child, choosing a consistent bedtime and waking time, and stopping caffeine and naps.

evidence.locator: Results › Response to Sleep Hygiene, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Sleep-onset latency fell from 91.7 to 69.3 minutes on diaries (t(28) = 2.77, p = .01) and from 98.1 to 73.0 on actigraphy (t(21) = 2.92, p < .01), effect size 0.67; diary variability fell from 47.7 to 29.1 minutes; five children met the response criterion (under 1 hour); clinicians rated 21% much or very much improved, 21% minimally improved and 54% unchanged; ADHD ratings did not change.

The abstract gives twenty-seven children receiving sleep hygiene; the participant flow gives 33 consenting, five withdrawing and five responding to sleep hygiene, leaving 23 eligible for randomization; this phase had no control group.

risk_of_bias.note: No control group; children selected for long sleep onset invite regression to the mean; parents knew the programme had begun.

inconsistency.note: Single study; diary and actigraph agree.

indirectness.note: Worded for the children and setting studied.

imprecision.note: About 28 children; the before-after change is precise but its cause is not.

grade.reasoning: An uncontrolled before-after comparison starts low; risk of bias −1 gives very low. Status single study.
